title: Volunteers, donated equipment, and the daily quartet rehearsals
summary: Volunteers supplied lights, a sound system and a piano; Decatur Street was then skid row. He explains how he, Willie T, George Davis and David Lee rehearsed daily, taping free and standard material, and their earlier New Orleans scene.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: And another amazing aspect of what happened with that is that Eugene had done this drawing on scale size, I mean drawing down a scale, and then he had measurements of how big this was supposed to be on this wall and how big this was supposed to be here and what colors were supposed to happen here. And they were very vivid at that time what we called day glow paints or things that were illuminated more so by black light or the purplish type of ultraviolet light that you see. And he brought in art students and architecture students from Tulane. And here again they took this thing and they traced this mural throughout the room and came in at different shifts. I mean it must have been for months of painting and bringing this thing into reality. But there also was a lady named Mona McMurray who was like a, I guess a magical mother or fairy godmother in a sense. I mean it looked like all the little things that you could think of that we didn't know how to get our hands on. Stage lighting and she had some old stage lights. She knew a friend that had these type of props. She knew somebody that had this to make this sound booth work together. And then there was a man named Gary Edwards who later had a musical supply house here. But we couldn't put together the kind of sound system that we needed. And at first he said, well I'll loan you one until you can get it together. And he said, no, I'll give you one. He designed a sound system for that room. And there was some speakers and all in the control booth set up the whole thing. There were some people here named, I think it was Carol and James Burns who connected with the museum. And there was a grand piano that was in very, very bad shape but that was of no use to them. That we could have gotten some work done to. Here came a grand piano for us to have in the jazz workshop. All of the various elements of things that were absolutely vital and essential to setting up a foundation to have this room vibrant and happening came together primarily through volunteers from every kind of walk of life. And Decatur Street at that time was, well it was the back of the French market in that particular section. There were a lot of derelicts and skid row type people all permeating through the whole area. And that particular end of Decatur Street was not even thought of as far as nightclubs or entertainment sort of thing. It was somewhat projected that they were going to do this renovation in the next couple of blocks next to Morning Call where Al Hurt later had a place that was developed there. But at the time that we were in the jazz workshop it was like no vision or no way could this happen. I think that that might have been part of the catalyst to people seeing some hope there. But the people that were really devout to the music, they didn't mind coming into the area. They didn't mind coming into contact with all the things that they would have to face en route to the jazz workshop. Because once you got in that door, once you got in, you knew that all the trouble you had taken to get there was worth it to get there. And also it welcomed you. And anybody that was, let's say, of a negative vibratory rate or not attuned to that music or not attuned to the love that was in that room, it seems like when they would walk in, they would hurry up and run out of there. This is the wrong place for me. These people are too unified or whatever. But it was a warm environment like that. And we had all kinds of people, a lot of college students, a lot of arts patrons that were just very curious because they knew that something new and something exciting was happening here. Also, we were playing a music at that time that we played some spontaneous improvisation or spontaneous compositions during that particular period of time. Willie T, who's my brother, George Davis and David Lee and myself, we would play together every day. We had been doing this for a couple of years at that point. Just about noon after getting up from a night, we'd work till like maybe 1, 2, 3 o'clock in the morning, get a good somewhat of a night's sleep. And around 11, 30, 12 o'clock, we would get together every day predominantly in George Davis' garage. We had a little small tape recorder, but we would just go in and play. Sometimes we would rehearse a specific tune, but oftentimes we would just tune into each other and just start playing. And sometimes this would go on for an hour, hour and a half, two hours. And we would segue from, say, maybe an original composition to something like Stella by Starlight or all the things you are. And then we'd go into some free or collective improvisation. But we were trying to include as many of the elements of standard jazz playing, rhythm changes, the blues. And at that time, I mean, like the Coltrane things that would be just becoming, which are standards now, I mean, things like Giant Steps, Moments Notice, all those kind of things. We were working on that kind of material and trying to learn how to play the standard repertoire. But we were also trying to incorporate some of these freer elements that was in some of Train's later music and Ornette Coleman's music. I mean, all of these influences were coming in. And the one thing that we tried to avoid was playing anybody else's statements or anything that they played. We tried to avoid playing anybody else's stuff verbatim. We might have played any like manner or like Ornette-ish or like the great group that Miles had during the late 60s with Tony and Ron and Herbie. And the magic that was happening in those rhythm sections. We were inspired by those things, but also trying to approach it from our own unique, intuitive kind of interpretation. That unless there was a real problem with what was happening musically, we tried to put it down on tape and just let it happen automatically or intuitively. And then go back and listen to the tapes and see what of this body of work we had just completed that we really liked, what we didn't like, what we wanted to keep. And when we recognized something that was very distinctly an element that we thought was unique and not like anybody else's stuff, then we would make a comment, well, we should include that in our playing from time to time. And when we do that, certain things we began to recognize. And the other thing that I'm more keenly aware of now is that we were playing some things that were so fresh and so new. This is some of the things that later Cannonball Adley would come in to record and also to talk about is that we were playing some new music that was unlike anything that I had heard other people play. And it was distinctively our music as well as when we wanted to play things that were of a common genre or that were popular in a jazz context that you knew that we were playing a train tune or that we were playing a Cannonball Adley tune or a Savonu tune or an Ornette tune. And the things that we were playing, the things that we were playing, we had not analyzed or no one had really analyzed. And we were awfully concerned, well, how do we explain what we're doing to someone else? And my brother, who's always had the, I mean, he's one of the most prolific composers I've ever met, but he does not directly read or write. He does not directly read or write. And stuff like pass this on or how to teach other young players to play that particular idiom or play those kind of things. And the period that we were putting this music together was also after, I mean, in my late high school years, say like 58, 59, going into 60, that was a very, there were some very vibrant things happening with Nat Parallot and Ellis and all those persons. And then during the very mid-60s, it seemed like most of those persons were either away and there was no real vibrant modern jazz stuff happening for a few years. I think Ellis might have been with Al Hurt during a particular period that we became very active, but those concerts that used to happen all the time were not happening so much then. And we said something has to be done to keep this alive and keep this, be at the forefront of creating some new New Orleans music to make not only ourselves constantly grow, but to inspire younger musicians to come up. Because I remember walking out River Road many, many nights from my parents' home on Monroe Street down to Oak Street and all the way out River Road to where Ellis had taken his home and transformed that into a place called the Music Haven. And it was like a very dreamlike jazz club. I mean, it was like my ideal kind of jazz club. He had his grand piano there, but he had taken what had been his house or his home and converted it into a place that was aesthetic as far as a room with good acoustics. James Black, Marshall Smith, Nat Parallot and Ellis. It was like going into a time warp. But when you consider what you encountered in all the other jazz settings or little places that were about, when you went there, you could just be suspended in a place where it was just heard nothing but wonderful music for two, three, four hours at a time. And that was an inspiration to me. But after that, there was a void, a period where there was very little happening for a while. And the closest thing that came to that was when Gloria De Freitas opened Gloria's jazz room on Roman in Spain that we played in, must have been about 65, 66, 67, like during that period. And then when that sort of faded out, I mean, she paid us extremely well, had all of the things that we needed. But yet again, it was in an alcohol environment or other things happening in and around clubs. And I was very inspired by Preservation Hall, which had, or it was another place on Bourbon Street. I think they might have called it Economy Hall or something during that time. But the thing about it was that no drinks. There were not drugs on the premises or it was just pure come in to hear the music, nothing elaborate. The thing that you came there to hear was the music. That's what you came for. And then afterwards, you went out for whatever libation or whatever kind of indulgences you wanted to do before or after. But when you came to that place, you came to hear just the music and the other things associated to the music. So I wanted to see an environment similar to that for the new music or for what I was terming during that particular time, the new New Orleans music or new New Orleans jazz. And to make an emphasis that whereas they were stressing preservation, we wanted to stress the evolution of the music. Because at one point we started to call it Evolution Hall or rather than a jazz workshop. But, you know...
